thesis.question: How do the systems behind selling fit together, why do the architectural decisions between them matter, and how do those decisions change as a business grows?
thesis.claim: A commerce platform is a promise-keeping machine: nearly every commerce failure is a promise one system made and another could not keep, so commerce architecture is the work of deciding which system may make which promise, how the others learn of it and what happens when they disagree, and the right decision changes with the shape and size of the business.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a commerce platform is a product a merchant selects, so that failures are the product's shortcomings and the remedy is a better or newer platform.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim spends its effort on ownership of facts and on the joins between systems, and stops expecting a replatforming to fix failures that were never inside the platform.
thesis.how_why: The storefront makes promises in seconds from copies of facts; a dozen systems owned by different teams and vendors keep them over days. Wherever a fact has no named record or a join has no owner, two systems can both be honest and still break the promise.

supporting_claims.claim: A commerce platform is the whole set of systems that make and keep promises, and its failures live in the joins between them.
Each promise (product, price, availability, payment, delivery, return) rests on facts that need exactly one owning system, with every other value a copy.
Each channel beyond the merchant's own shop adds promise-makers and writers the merchant does not control.
Separate systems behave like one only through designed joins: integration styles, events with reconciliation, contracts and shared identity.
What a merchant can promise is bounded by how the platforms it buys are built.
Security, privacy and regulation are promises imposed from outside that become requirements on the same systems.
The right assignment of promises changes with the business's shape, and should be changed at stage transitions rather than after incidents.
The public record of real companies supports these claims and shows where they stop applying.

flow.rationale: Parts II to IV follow one order in the sequence it happens (offer, commit, fulfil), so a newcomer always knows where they are; the scope then widens only after the single-shop path is complete. Evidence from real companies comes last, because the reader needs the vocabulary to read the cases critically. Moving the cases first would make them anecdotes; moving integration before fulfillment would explain joins between systems the reader has not met.

posts.title: Who Sells What to Whom: Business Models and the Economics That Shape Architecture
posts.question: Why do a D2C brand, a wholesaler, a retailer with stores, a marketplace seller and a marketplace operator need different systems, and why do a merchant's needs change as it grows?

know: The commerce business models and what each changes: who captures the order, sets the price, is the legal seller, holds the stock and ships.
The four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), defined by shape.

thesis.question: Why do a D2C brand, a wholesaler, a retailer with stores, a marketplace seller and a marketplace operator need different systems, and why do a merchant's needs change as it grows?
thesis.claim: They need different systems because a business model decides who captures the order, sets the price, is the legal seller, holds the stock and ships: a merchant needs a system for each promise it keeps itself and a connection for each it leaves to a partner. Growth changes the need by shape, not revenue: each added channel, stock location, country or brand adds systems holding copies of the same orders and stock.

thesis.so_what: A merchant that copies the architecture of a company with a different model or shape buys problems it does not have and leaves its own unsolved.
thesis.how_why: A promise needs a system that can keep it: the legal seller must issue invoices and refunds, the stock holder must keep availability true, the shipper must book carriers and report tracking. Who holds each role therefore sets which systems a merchant runs and which partner systems it connects to, and each copy added by growth is one more join that must be kept in step.

The four ways merchants assign ownership and when each stops fitting.

'Single source of truth' means one record per fact, not one system for every fact.

Tell, from the writer list, whether a claimed system of record is one.

posts.title: Suites, SaaS, Open Source and Composable: The Platform Landscape in 2026
posts.question: What separates the kinds of commerce platform on sale in 2026, how are they priced, and what changed in the market between 2023 and 2026?

know: Seven platform categories and where each puts the integration work and the cost.
That most platforms are priced on the merchant's sales, with dated figures.
believe: A platform category moves integration work; it does not remove it.
can_do: Read a vendor's 2026 pitch as a layer to add or a move to make, and say who would carry the work afterwards.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two platforms with the same feature list, the reader names three operating-model differences to ask about before comparing features.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two platforms both offer cart, catalog and checkout. What would you ask before comparing features?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Who runs hosting and upgrades; how the price moves with sales; who carries integration and what leaving costs.

thesis.question: What separates the kinds of commerce platform on sale in 2026, how are they priced, and what changed in the market between 2023 and 2026?
thesis.claim: The seven categories (hosted SaaS, enterprise suite, open source, composable, ERP-centered, specialist layer, specialist group) differ less in features than in who hosts, upgrades and integrates: each moves the integration work rather than removing it. Their prices follow the merchant's sales more than the software. From 2023 to 2026 suite and composable vendors began selling modules that sit beside an existing stack: layers to add, not reasons to move.
thesis.disputed_by: Feature comparisons that rank platforms by what they can do, and vendor claims that one category (composable, suite or hosted) is the modern answer worth moving to.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that replatforms to escape integration work finds the same work on the other side, under a different owner and price; one that reads a pitch as a layer can add it without moving.
thesis.how_why: Hosted platforms push variation to apps, suites keep integration inside one data model, open source moves hosting and upgrades to the merchant, composable moves integration to the merchant, ERP-centered commerce keeps it inside the ERP, and specialist layers and groups leave it on the connectors to the merchant's platform. Vendors charge where they sit in the payment path, through payment fees and plans set by gross merchandise value, so the bill follows sales. And when replatforming demand softened, as Commerce.com reported, suite and composable vendors repackaged their products as modules that attach to a stack the merchant already runs.

parts.title: Part II — CATALOG: Products, Prices and Promises

know: The four kinds of fact a shopper reads before buying (product content, price, discount, availability), how fast each changes and which kind of system owns each.
That the search index and the listings on channels the merchant does not run are copies of those facts.
believe: Product content, price, discount and availability need separate owners and separate paths to the channels, although they appear side by side on one product page.
A value shown from a copy that nothing compares with its source is a promise the merchant cannot be sure of keeping.
can_do: For product content, price, discount and stock at their own company, name the system of record, who may write it, how each channel learns of a change and what compares the channel's copy with the source.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given a channel that shows a different price and a different stock status from the merchant's own shop, a reader who has read only Part II treats them as two facts with two owners and asks about the source and the comparison of each copy, before asking for a faster synchronization or a new product.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace listing shows a jacket at last week's campaign price and 'in stock'; the merchant's own shop shows the list price and 'sold out'. Using only Part II: which facts are involved, and what would you ask about each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Two facts, price and availability, with different owners. The listing is a copy of each. For each: which system is the source, when and how the listing last learned of a change (an effective-dated price change; a stock event or a scheduled push), and what compares the listing with the source. Not 'synchronize faster' and not 'replace the connector'.

thesis.question: Which system should own each fact a shopper reads before buying (the product's description, its price, a discount, its stock status), and how should each fact reach the channels and the search results that show it?
thesis.claim: The four facts need four owners, not one catalog, because they do not change together (content changes by the season, a price by the day, a discount with each cart, stock by the second): product content is owned attribute by attribute in the system where its producing team works, a price by the system whose rule selects it, a discount by the cart that computes it, and stock status by one service that derives it from counted stock and commitments. A channel that can ask the owner at the moment of sale asks it; the search index and every other channel receive a copy of each fact, and a copy is safe to show only if it names its source and is compared with that source on a schedule set by how fast the fact changes.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the catalog is one record in one product, the shop platform or a product information system, which holds description, price, discount and stock together and pushes them to every channel on one schedule.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers four ownership questions before it buys a product information system, a pricing service, a search service or a faster connector, and adds a comparison of copy against source to every feed it keeps; Kestrel & Pine's Price Drift ran for nine days, and its Black Friday Oversell for an evening, because no such comparison existed.
thesis.how_why: A description may be a day old without harm, a price that is a day old is charged to real orders, a discount depends on a cart that does not exist until the shopper builds it, and the last unit can be sold in seconds; one update schedule is therefore too slow for stock or needlessly strict for content. A channel that holds its own listing cannot ask the owner at the moment of sale, so it shows a copy, and a pushed update that is lost raises no error anywhere: only a comparison finds it.

supporting_claims.claim: Product data needs one owning system per attribute, not per product, and identifiers (SKU, GTIN) that are never changed or reused, because orders, warehouses and marketplaces are keyed on them.
A price is selected from several valid candidates by one written rule, once, at order placement, and frozen on the order; the invoice and any refund copy that frozen price.

A discount is computed once, in the cart, in a declared order of evaluation with a stop rule, and is finished only when it is allocated to the order lines that invoices and refunds read; gift cards and loyalty points are balances the merchant owes, not discounts.
The search index owns no fact: it is a copy of product, price, availability and review data, so what a shopper can find is decided by what is fed into the index and how fresh each feed is.
'In stock' is a number derived from counted stock and commitments, each with one writer; it is computed in one place and published to the channels, not stored as a fact by each of them.
A channel that cannot ask the owning system at the moment of sale shows a copy, and a copy is safe to show only with a named source and a scheduled comparison against it.

role.contribution: Applies the record-and-copy rule to the facts that exist before an order: product, price, promotion, search index and availability.

additional_patterns.applies_to: product-information to commerce-promotions: one variant, then the prices that variant can carry, then the discounts on a cart of several variants

flow.rationale: Each chapter uses what the one before it fixed. Prices are stored per SKU, so the product chapter's identifiers come first; a discount is subtracted from a selected price, so pricing precedes promotions; the search index is a copy of product, price and discount data, so it follows the three chapters that say who owns them; it also copies stock status, which the search chapter treats only as a figure that goes out of date and leaves to the next chapter; availability comes last because the search chapter ends on a results page that says 'in stock' from a two-hour-old copy, which is the question the inventory chapter answers, and because its last step, committing one unit to one order at checkout, is where Part III begins. Putting inventory before search would remove that one forward reference, but the part would then end on search instead of on the unit committed at checkout. Moving search first would describe a copy before the reader knows what it copies or who owns the originals; moving inventory before pricing would cut the price-to-discount sequence in two and put the commitment at checkout four chapters away from the cart chapter that relies on it.

closing.synthesis: The season typed four times, the Price Drift, the Stacking Bug, the jacket nobody could find and the Oversell look like five problems in five tools. Read together they are one: a value shown or used by a system that did not own it, with nothing comparing it to the system that did. closing.callback: The part opening's product page, where a description, a price and a stock badge sit side by side and change at different speeds.

takeaway.content: For product content, price, discount and stock, write down the owner, who may write, how each channel learns of a change and what compares the copy with the source; start with stock, the fact that changes fastest.

posts.title: What Does It Cost? Price Lists, Contract Prices, Currencies and Tax
posts.question: Where should a price be computed, and how do you keep it consistent across storefronts, stores, marketplaces and wholesale?

know: What a price is made of: price lists and the dimensions (market, currency, customer group, channel, quantity, validity, tax basis) on which candidates differ.
The selection rule, the moment of selection, and the difference between the engine that selects a price and the copies that show it.
The two EU rules that make price history a legal record: tax-inclusive consumer prices and the lowest price of the previous 30 days.

A copy of a price is a promise made on the source's behalf, so it needs a source, an effective date and a comparison.
can_do: For one product at their own company, list every system that holds a price and name the source for each kind of price.
Say, for a given channel, whether it can call the pricing engine or must receive a copy, and what the copy then needs.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a channel that still shows an ended campaign price, the reader names a lost or dropped update to a copy as the failure and a scheduled comparison of copy against source as what detects it.

acceptance_criteria.expected: The price selected once, at order placement, by the same rule and data the storefront uses, so the list price that applies after the campaign; it is frozen on the order, and the invoice copies it and never selects again.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a pricing system must be able to answer before a price reduction is announced in the EU.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant in the Netherlands plans to announce '20% off' next week. Using only this chapter: what must its pricing system be able to answer first, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The lowest price it charged for that product in that market in the previous 30 days, because EU law (Directive 2019/2161) requires an announced reduction to show that prior price; this needs a price history with effective dates.

acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What a price is made of and the rule that selects one; tax, markets and currencies; the European price rules; the engine against the copies and who may change a price; the choices and their trade-offs by scale stage; platform documentation and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 design; how pricing fails. thesis.question: Where should a price be computed, and how do you keep it consistent across storefronts, stores, marketplaces and wholesale?
thesis.claim: A price should be computed by one written, deterministic rule that selects it from the valid candidates, and each kind of price (consumer, wholesale) should have one source system, the system in which the team that sets that kind of price works; the price is selected once, at order placement, and frozen on the order for the invoice and any refund to copy. A channel that can call the rule at the moment of sale, such as the merchant's own storefront, calls it; a channel that cannot (a marketplace listing, a store till that must work offline, a wholesale customer's electronic order) receives a copy, and the copies stay consistent only if each carries its source and an effective date and is compared with that source every day, with each difference listed for a person to correct.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a price is a number stored on the product, so that keeping channels consistent means typing or pushing the same number into every system, and pushing it more often when they disagree.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's German storefront sold at €179 instead of €199 for nine days, on 410 orders, at a cost of about €8,200, because the update that should have restored the price failed and nothing compared the channels. With a dated campaign row and a daily comparison the difference is on a list the next morning; and a merchant that keeps dated prices can answer the EU's question about the lowest price of the last 30 days.
thesis.how_why: One SKU has several valid prices that differ by market, customer group, channel, quantity and validity, so only a rule can pick one; two systems that apply different rules, or the same rule at different moments, charge different amounts for the same sale. A pushed price change can be lost without an error in the sender or the receiver, so a missing update is found only by comparing the copy with the source.

role.contribution: Shows that a catalog fact can be the result of a rule and a moment, not a stored value, and introduces the engine-against-copies distinction that the promotions, search and inventory chapters reuse.

transition_in.carries_over: The product described once and owned per attribute, with price and stock left out of the ownership table.
transition_in.introduces: A product-related fact that changes on a different cadence, carries legal weight in Europe and is copied into more systems than any other: the price.

posts.title: Discounts, Coupons and Loyalty: Promotions Without Chaos
posts.question: How do you offer discounts, coupons, bundles and loyalty rewards without breaking the price, the margin or the books?

know: The parts of a promotion system: definitions with an order of evaluation and a stop rule, eligibility, the code ledger, evaluation in the cart, allocation to order lines.
Why gift cards, store credit and loyalty points are liabilities held in ledgers and not promotions.
believe: A promotion incident is a governance failure (a setting without an owner) before it is a software failure.
The allocated net line price, not the list price, is the price every later system must read.
can_do: Allocate an order-level discount to lines and compute the refund for one returned line.
Ask of any promotion setup which system computes the final discount, in what order, where stacking stops and who may change that.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an order with an order-level discount and one returned line, the reader computes the refund from the allocated net line price and says what had to be recorded at order time.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order holds a €199 jacket and €36 of socks, with a 10% code on the whole order. The customer returns the jacket. Using only this chapter: how much is refunded, and what must have been recorded when the order was placed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: €179.10, not €199: the €23.50 discount is allocated to the lines in proportion (€19.90 to the jacket), and the net price per line is written to the order, where the returns tool, the invoice and the credit note read it.

acceptance_criteria.probe: In a sale week a welcome code combined with an automatic 20% discount on the same carts, although nobody intended it. Using only this chapter: what was missing, and what would you do before the next campaign?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The rule that decides stacking lived in a platform setting that nobody owned or checked against the campaign plan. Give the combination settings one owner, write each campaign with its order of evaluation and stop rule in one calendar, and test the new campaign against every promotion already active. Governance first, not a new promotion engine.

acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why is a gift card not a promotion, and who has to check its balance against what, how often?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It is value the customer has paid for in advance, so the merchant owes it: a liability kept as a ledger with a balance. Finance reconciles the stored-value balances to a liability account every month.

acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What a promotion is and what it touches; the parts of a promotion system and where the final discount is computed; how a discount reaches the invoice, the refund and the books; gift cards, store credit and points as ledgers; the choices by scale stage; dated examples and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 plan; how promotions fail. Evidence: the Black Friday Stacking Bug, a worked allocation on Eva's order, platform documentation, accounting standards and a company filing.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do you offer discounts, coupons, bundles and loyalty rewards without breaking the price, the margin or the books?
thesis.claim: Promotions leave the price, the margin and the books intact when three things hold: each promotion, whether a discount, a coupon or a bundle, is a data record with a place in a declared order of evaluation and a rule that says where stacking (combining promotions on one order) stops; the final discount is computed once, in the cart, and written to the order allocated to its lines, so that invoices and refunds read the net price of each line; and gift cards, store credit and loyalty points are kept apart from promotions as ledgers of value the merchant owes its customers, reconciled every month to a liability account.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a promotion is a marketing setting a campaign manager switches on in the shop platform, that the discount shown on the product page is the discount, and that a gift card or a loyalty point is one more kind of discount.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday Stacking Bug put two discounts on 2,860 orders and cost about €52,000, part of it refunded twice on returns. A merchant that accepts the claim gives the combination settings one owner, tests each campaign against the promotions already active, and makes its order export carry the net price per line.
thesis.how_why: Two promotions that are each valid combine unless a rule says where stacking stops; when that rule is a platform setting nobody owns, nobody checks it against a new campaign. The product page is rendered before the cart exists, so it can only estimate; the cart is the first place where all lines, codes and the customer are known. Invoices, tax, returns and partial refunds work line by line, so a discount left at order level is refunded at the wrong amount. A gift-card balance is money already received for goods not yet delivered, and a loyalty point is a reward the customer has already earned, so accounting standards record both as liabilities.

role.contribution: Shows what may be subtracted from a selected price and how the result is fixed on the order, so that the price a later system reads is the one the customer paid.

transition_in.carries_over: The price selected by rule and frozen on the order.
transition_in.introduces: What may be subtracted from that price at checkout, in which order, and how the discount reaches the invoice and the refund.

posts.title: Finding the Product: Search, Navigation and Merchandising

Which facts belong in the index and which are fetched from their owner at query time, and why.
That reviews are data in the index with provenance the law requires a merchant to keep.

Synonyms, merchandising rules and ranking parameters are data with owners and end dates, not settings in a vendor's console.

Decide, for a given fact, whether it goes in the index or is fetched at query time, from how fast it changes.

acceptance_criteria.expected: How the review was collected and the order it came from, because EU law (Directive 2019/2161) requires a merchant to be able to show that reviews come from real purchasers and to take steps to check.

thesis.question: How do shoppers find products, and what has to be true of the data for search to work?
thesis.claim: Shoppers find products by search, by navigation and by recommendation, and all three read one search index, which is a copy of product, price, availability and review data. Search works when three things are true of that data: the attributes and the words shoppers use are in the index; each feed into the index is refreshed at least as often as the statement shown from that feed (a price, a rating) can change; and a fact that no feed can keep that fresh, such as the last unit of stock, is fetched at query time from the system that owns the fact.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that poor search results are a weakness of the search engine, to be cured by buying a stronger search product or adding AI retrieval.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's rate of searches with no result fell from 9.4% to 4.1% after it added synonym sets and one product attribute, with the search engine it already had. A merchant that accepts the claim measures its failing queries, pays for product attributes and a stock feed before it pays a search vendor, and stops showing an exact stock count from the index.
thesis.how_why: An engine can match, filter and rank only on what its index holds: a waterproof rating kept in a spreadsheet cannot match 'waterproof jacket', and a stock figure copied every hour keeps saying 'in stock' after the shelf is empty. Ranking, merchandising rules and semantic retrieval all run on those same index records, so none of them can supply an attribute that was never loaded or correct a figure that is out of date. A value fetched at query time is the owning system's current value, so it cannot be out of date in the way an indexed copy can.

transition_in.carries_over: Product content, price and discount, each with a named owner.
transition_in.introduces: A system that owns none of those facts and shows copies of all of them: the search index through which the shopper finds the product.

posts.title: Is It in Stock? Inventory, Availability and the Promise You Can Keep
posts.question: What does "in stock" mean, who computes it, and how do you avoid selling what you do not have?

know: The five stock numbers (on hand, committed, reserved, held back, incoming) and the available-to-promise figure derived from them.
The three moments at which a unit can become promised (cart, order, fulfillment) and what each costs.
The parts of an availability service and which system writes which number.
believe: 'Available' is a computation that no system should store as a fact and let another overwrite.
Oversells come from several writers and from scheduled copying, not from a system that cannot count.
can_do: Compute available-to-promise from on hand, committed, reserved and held-back units.
Name, for their own company, the system of record for on hand at each location and the only writer of committed.
Say when a merchant needs a separate availability service.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the stock numbers for one product at one location, the reader computes what a channel may still sell and names the result as derived.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A warehouse has 10 jackets on the shelf. 3 belong to placed orders that have not shipped, 1 is reserved in a cart, and 2 are held back as a buffer. Using only this chapter: how many may a channel still sell, and what is that number called?
acceptance_criteria.expected: 4: on hand minus committed minus reserved minus held back. It is available-to-promise (or 'available'), a derived number, not a count.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two channels that sold the same last unit, the reader names several writers and scheduled copying as causes and does not accept a shorter sync interval as the whole remedy.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two channels sold the same last unit. Using only this chapter: which causes would you look for, and would copying stock every five minutes instead of every hour fix it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Several systems writing the same stock number; copying on a schedule, so each channel learns of the other's sales late; a reservation window; a wrong count; no buffer. A shorter interval shortens the lag and leaves the writers. The remedy is one writer for on hand and one for committed, stock changes sent as events, 'available' computed in one place per channel with a buffer, and a reconciliation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say which interaction must get an exact answer from the availability service and which may read a slightly stale copy.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which step of a purchase must ask the availability service and wait for the answer, and which steps may show a slightly old figure?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Checkout, at order creation: the unit is committed atomically so the last unit goes to exactly one order. The 'in stock' badge on listing pages, add to cart and the marketplace stock push may read a slightly stale copy.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What 'in stock' means as several numbers; when a unit becomes promised; many locations and channels; the availability service and what each interaction needs; events against scheduled copying; the choices and their trade-offs by scale stage; Kestrel & Pine's Oversell worked through; how stock integrations fail. Evidence: the Black Friday Oversell, platform documentation, a study of inventory record accuracy.

thesis.question: What does "in stock" mean, who computes it, and how do you avoid selling what you do not have?
thesis.claim: 'In stock' means available-to-promise: units on hand minus three amounts: units committed to orders, units held temporarily for carts, and units held back as a buffer. This figure is computed in one place and published to each channel: by the shop platform while the shop platform is the only system that takes orders and counts stock, and, once a second system takes orders or counts stock, by one service that receives every count and every commitment. A merchant avoids selling what it does not have by giving on hand and committed one writer each, sending each stock change as an event when it happens instead of copying totals on a schedule, holding back a buffer per channel, and committing a unit to exactly one order at checkout.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that stock is one number which each system holds and synchronizes with the others, so that an oversell is cured by synchronizing more often.
thesis.so_what: On Black Friday 2026 Kestrel & Pine oversold 1,340 units on 1,120 orders, at a cost of about €96,000, while every system was up and reporting its own number. A merchant that accepts the claim writes down who owns each stock number before it builds the first connector.
thesis.how_why: A stored 'available' figure can be overwritten by any system that copies it, so two writers, or one copy made on a schedule, leave channels selling from different answers; at Kestrel & Pine's peak of 38 orders a minute, a one-hour copy interval can hide up to about 2,300 orders from the other channels. Deriving the figure in one place, from one counted fact and one list of commitments, leaves one answer for every channel, and only the commit at checkout has to be exact.

role.contribution: Applies the part's argument to the fastest-changing fact, where a stale copy costs most, and performs the part's closing before handing the committed unit to the cart.

transition_in.carries_over: A search result that shows the jacket 'in stock' from a copy of stock up to two hours old.
transition_in.introduces: What 'in stock' means, who computes it, and how the figure becomes a promise the warehouse can keep.

parts.title: Part III — ORDER: Cart, Checkout, Payment and the Order Record

know: The owners one order passes through after the cart: checkout creates it, the payment provider decides whether money moved, the order record holds its status, and the ERP issues its invoice and keeps the books.
Why the order keeps three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns) and why every message and request about it carries a business key.
believe: Checkout, the payment provider, the order record and the ERP each hold a different truth about the same order, and they agree only where each handoff has one writer, a key and a comparison.
The thank-you page, a single status field and a refund button in a provider's console are not evidence that money moved or that an order is complete.
can_do: For one order at their own company, name the system that creates it, the one that knows whether it is paid, the one that holds its status per shipment and the one that issues its invoice, and the key and the comparison at each handoff.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given an order whose systems disagree about its delivery, its invoice and its refund, a reader who has read only Part III names a missing status line, writer, key or comparison for each disagreement, before naming a better connector or a new product.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer paid by iDEAL for two items that left in two parcels. After the first parcel arrives, the shop says 'Delivered', the warehouse 'In picking' and the ERP 'Not invoiced'. She later returns an item, and both the returns portal and a support agent in the payment provider's console refund it. Using only Part III: what was missing in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The order had one status word instead of separate status lines with the goods status per shipment, so the first parcel's delivery marked the whole order delivered; the invoice waited for 'order complete' instead of being issued per shipment at dispatch, and nothing listed shipped orders without an invoice; two systems could refund and the request carried no business key (the return id), so the provider paid twice, and a daily comparison of the provider's refunds with credit notes would have found it. Not 'a better connector', 'a new payment provider' or 'an OMS' alone.

thesis.question: How does a shopper's cart become an order, and what keeps the systems that hold the order, its money and its books in agreement afterwards?
thesis.claim: A cart becomes an order once, at checkout, which asks each system that owns a fact for a final answer, writes those answers (price, tax, availability, delivery promise) into the order and creates it exactly once; afterwards the order, its money and its books stay in agreement only under four rules: the order has one home with three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns), moved only by messages from the systems that witnessed each payment, shipment or return; every message and request about the order carries a business key that makes a repeat harmless, and whatever is still unresolved is checked with its source on a schedule; every action that moves money or issues a legal document has one writing system; and invoices, payout reports and bank lines are matched line by line every month on identifiers the order passes along.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the order is the shop platform's record with one status, that the thank-you page, the payment connector and the ERP connector between them keep the order, the money and the books in agreement, and that a disagreement is fixed by a better connector, a second payment provider or an order management system.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order (#1052877: 'Delivered', 'In picking' and 'Not invoiced' for six days, 11 support tickets) and its Double Refund (212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice) were not faults inside any one product: each was a missing status line, writer, key or comparison. A merchant that accepts the claim writes down the order's home, the writer and the key of each money action and the monthly match before it buys an order management system or adds a payment provider.
thesis.how_why: From the moment the shopper leaves for her bank's app, the merchant's own systems no longer witness what happens: the payment provider knows whether money moved, the warehouse which lines left, the carrier which parcel arrived, and each reports by message, which can be late, out of order, repeated or lost. One status word lets the latest message overwrite the others; a request without a business key cannot be told from a retry, so a second writer or one retry moves money twice; and an invoice, which must be numbered consecutively and never edited, can come from only one system. A payout nets payments, refunds and fees from different days, so only a line-by-line match on shared identifiers shows that nothing was lost.

supporting_claims.claim: Checkout owns none of the facts it writes into the order: it asks each owning system for a final answer at the moment of commitment, so an answer taken from an out-of-date copy becomes an error that every later system inherits.

After checkout the order's systems learn what happened from messages sent by the systems that witnessed it (the payment provider, the warehouse, the carrier), which arrive late, out of order, twice or not at all; every message and request therefore carries a business key that makes a repeat harmless, and a scheduled job asks the source about everything still unresolved.
Every action that moves money or issues a legal document has exactly one writing system: one system may refund, one may capture, and one system per legal entity issues invoices and credit notes.

An order is one record with three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns) from which the status the customer sees is computed, and once orders are created and fulfilled in several places one system must hold that record as the order's home.

Tax is computed from facts the shop owns (ship-to address, product tax category, buyer status) under rates kept once for every channel, and the invoice is issued per shipment at dispatch, never edited and corrected only by a credit note that references it.

The ledger is posted from documents and payout reports, not from payment events, and the books agree with the shop only when invoices, payout reports and bank lines are matched line by line on shared identifiers.

posts.title: From Cart to Confirmation: Checkout Orchestration
posts.question: What happens between "add to cart" and "order confirmed", and why do platforms restrict what merchants may change in checkout?

know: The difference between a cart (a draft that reserves and promises nothing), checkout (a clocked sequence that asks for final answers) and the order (the record the rest of the platform must keep).
What checkout calls, in what order, and how fresh each answer must be.
The four ways to run a checkout, and the mechanisms through which platforms let merchants change it.

The payment provider's signed message, not the thank-you page, decides that a payment succeeded.

Judge a proposal to customize checkout by its mechanism and by the vendor's support date for that mechanism.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a shopper who pays in her bank's app and never returns, and a payment notification delivered twice, the reader says when the order is created, what marks it paid and why the repeat changes nothing.

acceptance_criteria.expected: Checkout trusted the availability answer it was given, which came from the platform's copy of stock refreshed up to two hours earlier; checkout owns no stock figure. acceptance_criteria.expected: Use a sanctioned extension point of the platform, which runs with a time limit and is versioned. A third-party script on the payment page falls under the card industry's script rules (PCI DSS) and can read every card number typed there, and a mechanism outside the sanctioned ones is withdrawn on a date the vendor announces (Shopify's checkout.liquid and Scripts); keep an inventory of each customization, its mechanism and the vendor's support date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?

Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's checkout, vendor documentation, Shopify's dated changelog.

thesis.question: What happens between "add to cart" and "order confirmed", and why do platforms restrict what merchants may change in checkout?
thesis.claim: Between 'add to cart' and 'order confirmed', checkout asks each system that owns a fact for a final answer (price, tax, availability, delivery promise, payment), writes those answers into the order and creates the order exactly once, keyed on the cart and the payment rather than on a page load, leaving the payment provider's signed message, not the thank-you page, to mark it paid. Platforms restrict merchant changes to named extension points with time limits because every order passes through checkout: merchant code there can delay or fail order creation at peak, a script on the payment page can read the card numbers typed into it, and a template the merchant edits cannot follow the platform's upgrades.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that checkout is the storefront's last few pages, which a merchant or its agency may edit like any other page, and that the order exists, paid, once the shopper reaches the thank-you page.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's checkout kept selling the Ridgewalker jacket for up to two hours after Duiven ran out on Black Friday 2026 because checkout wrote the answer of an out-of-date stock copy into each order and the warehouse could not keep those orders; the fix is to have a current availability service answer that call, not to change checkout. A merchant that accepts the claim lists what its checkout calls and which answers come from copies, creates orders keyed on the cart and the payment and settles them by webhook and a daily job, and customizes checkout only through sanctioned extension points listed with the vendor's support date; Shopify withdrew editable checkout templates and scripts on dated deadlines between August 2024 and August 2026.
thesis.how_why: The warehouse, finance and the customer all act on what checkout writes into the order, so a stale price or stock figure written there becomes their error. The shopper leaves for her bank's app or a 3-D Secure challenge and may not come back, and the provider's webhook arrives late, out of order or twice, so an order created on the thank-you page can be lost and one created per request without a key can be duplicated. Checkout carries every order at peak load and its payment page falls under the card industry's script rules, so code the platform cannot limit in time or isolate puts every order at risk; and the platform ships its own checkout changes (new payment methods, compliance fixes) into its template, so a merchant's edited copy misses them. Webhooks can also stop arriving, so a daily job asks the provider about every order still pending.

transition_in.introduces: What checkout calls, in what order, and how it creates the order exactly once.

posts.title: Taking the Money: Payment Providers, Authorization, Capture and Refunds
posts.question: How does money move from the shopper to the merchant, and what can go wrong?

know: The parties to a payment (shopper, issuer, scheme, acquirer, payment provider) and its four stages: authorization, capture, settlement, payout; refunds and chargebacks as payments flowing back.
How payment methods differ by country (iDEAL, Bancontact, PayPal and purchase on account) and what each difference changes in the design.
What strong customer authentication, 3-D Secure, the liability shift and PCI DSS scope require of the payment design.

A refund is a new payment, not an undo, and needs one writer and one key.
can_do: Name, for their own company, every system that holds a credential to refund, capture or create a payment, and the business key each request carries.
Say what a daily payment reconciliation compares and what it finds.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given returns refunded twice by two systems, the reader explains why the provider accepted the second refund and names the three controls that prevent it, before naming a new provider.

acceptance_criteria.expected: Two systems could refund and neither request carried a key naming the return, so the provider saw two valid requests. The controls: one writer per money action (the returns portal through the platform, the console read-only for everyone else); the return id as the refund's idempotency key; a daily comparison of the provider's refunds with the refunds the platform recorded. Not a new provider.

acceptance_criteria.expected: The authorization (valid about seven days for the major card schemes) has expired, so the funds were released and the capture fails; the parcel leaves unpaid. acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why can a Dutch shop not reuse its card payment design unchanged for iDEAL?
acceptance_criteria.expected: iDEAL is an instant, irrevocable transfer from the shopper's bank with no separate capture and no chargeback, and a 15-minute session; a refund is a new transfer back. A card is authorized, then captured inside a window, and can be disputed. A design that assumes one method's stages breaks on the other.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?

thesis.question: How does money move from the shopper to the merchant, and what can go wrong?
thesis.claim: Money moves in four stages that the merchant only requests and the shopper's bank, the card or bank scheme and the payment provider carry out: authorization reserves the amount, capture takes it, settlement moves it between banks, and payout pays the merchant net batches on the provider's schedule, typically one per sales day; a refund or a chargeback is a new payment in the opposite direction, and each payment method changes the stages (an iDEAL payment is taken at once and cannot be charged back; a card authorization expires after about seven days). The failures that land on the merchant's own systems are acting on an outcome it did not see or moving money twice: an order marked paid or unpaid without the provider's confirmed message, a capture attempted after the authorization has expired, and one refund sent by two systems with no shared key.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that payments are the payment provider's concern: once a provider is integrated, 'paid' is a flag set at checkout, a refund is an undo anyone with console access may perform, and the main payment decision is which provider to use or whether to add a second one.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine refunded 212 returns twice in January 2027, €19,400, because the returns portal and support in the provider's console could both refund and neither request carried a key; bank-transfer refunds could not be recalled. Its fix was one writer, the return id as the key and a daily comparison, not a new provider. A merchant that accepts the claim lists who holds a credential to move money and with what key before it compares providers, and keeps one provider with that discipline until volume, countries or resilience require more.
thesis.how_why: The issuer and the provider decide whether money moved and report it by webhook, which arrives at least once, in no guaranteed order, and stops retrying after 26 hours (Mollie) or three days (Stripe), so only the provider's record, fetched when the decision matters, and a daily job for pending payments give the order the true state. A provider executes every valid request it receives; a refund that names only an order and an amount cannot be recognized as a repeat, whereas a request carrying the return id as its idempotency key returns the first result. An authorization lapses on the issuer's clock whatever the order's status, so a capture must be scheduled against that deadline; and each method fixes its own windows, so a design built on one method's stages misses another's deadlines.

role.contribution: Follows the money the order is waiting for through stages the merchant does not control and makes the single writer and the business key the rule for every action that moves money.

The order's three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns) and how the status the customer sees is computed from them.
Routing, split shipments and backorders, and what an order management system holds and what it leaves to the shop platform and the ERP.

Not decided by revenue.

acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?

thesis.question: Where does the order live once it is placed, what states does it pass through, and when does a merchant need an order management system (OMS)?
thesis.claim: Once placed, an order should live in one system that holds it as one record, under one order number, with three separate status lines (money: authorized, paid, refunded, moved by the payment provider's events; goods: requested, accepted, shipped, delivered, held per shipment and moved by the warehouse and the carrier; returns: requested, received, inspected, refunded or exchanged) and computes the status the customer sees from all its shipments, so that the order reads delivered only when every parcel has been delivered. While one channel creates orders and one location fulfils them, that system is the shop platform; a merchant needs an OMS as the order's home once at least two of four conditions hold (several channels create orders, several locations fulfil them, promises depend on the location, service agents cannot see one order across systems), because an OMS, unlike the ERP, can route lines between locations and answer a customer's question about a parcel.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that an order has one status in whichever system took it, kept in step with the others by connectors, and that an OMS is a product for large retailers, needed by revenue or order volume rather than by how many systems create and fulfil orders.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 read 'Delivered' in the platform, 'In picking' in the warehouse and 'Not invoiced' in the ERP while the customer had a fleece and no socks, and produced 11 support tickets; with goods status per shipment it would have read 'Partially delivered: 1 of 2 parcels'. Kestrel & Pine meets all four conditions, so under W2 it makes a bought OMS the order hub, with the platform keeping the checkout and the ERP the books. A merchant that accepts the claim counts its order sources and fulfilling locations and names the order's home before it buys anything.
thesis.how_why: Money, goods and returns are changed by different systems at different times (the payment provider, the warehouse and the carrier per parcel, the returns portal), so one status word lets the latest message overwrite the others: one parcel's delivery scan marked a two-parcel order delivered. Every system that copies the order receives it at least once, so the copies stay one order only through one number family with the order number as the key. With one channel and one location the platform's record sees every change; with several sources, each with its own connector to the warehouse and the books, no system sees the whole order; one condition alone can be handled by the platform plus a connector, but two make the joins between systems the problem, and choosing which location ships which line needs rules over stock, capacity, cut-off times and cost that the platforms' priority and distance rules do not hold. The ERP holds the financial record and runs in batches, so it cannot answer a parcel question.

role.contribution: Gives the order one home and separate status lines, so that the payment outcome, each parcel and each return are kept without overwriting each other, and supplies the per-shipment record the ledger chapter invoices from.

transition_in.introduces: The rest of the order's life after 'paid': the goods and returns that move on their own status lines, the systems that hold copies of the order, and which of them is its home.

posts.question: How does an order become tax, an invoice and entries in the books, and what does the commerce system owe finance?

The VAT rules that decide a rate: destination rates above the €10,000 One Stop Shop threshold, the reverse charge for EU business buyers with a valid VAT number, and tax-inclusive against tax-exclusive prices.
The ledger entries for a consumer order paid through a payment provider, and why Kestrel & Pine recognizes revenue for goods at delivery.

acceptance_criteria.expected: The payout is net of fees and of refunds and chargebacks from earlier days, and arrives days later. Finance matches it line by line, using the order number passed to the provider and the batch or trace reference on the bank line, and posts fees from the report; matching totals only cannot find a missing line.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why the amount reaching the bank differs from what the customer paid; following the VAT in Eva's order into the ERP; a Belgian wholesale invoice over Peppol; tax, invoices, credit notes, ledger entries and reconciliation. thesis.question: How does an order become tax, an invoice and entries in the books, and what does the commerce system owe finance?
thesis.claim: An order becomes tax, an invoice and ledger entries through documents, not events: the tax is computed from three facts the shop owns (the ship-to address, the product's tax category, and whether the buyer is a consumer or a VAT-registered business) under rates kept in one place for every channel; the invoice is issued at dispatch for each shipment by one system per legal entity, numbered in one consecutive series, never edited and corrected only by a credit note that references it; and the ledger is posted from invoices, credit notes and the payment provider's payout reports. The commerce system owes finance the facts and identifiers those documents need (the tax basis frozen on the order, a shipment confirmation carrying the shipment id, the buyer references an e-invoice must carry, the order number passed to the payment provider, refunds from one writer), so that a monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines explains each difference.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the shop platform's order confirmation is the invoice, that tax is a rate the platform adds at checkout, and that the books can be posted from the platform's payment events as they arrive, with differences found by comparing monthly totals.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 sat 'Not invoiced' for six days because the invoice waited for an 'order complete' message that a short pick prevented and no report listed shipped orders without an invoice; the Double Refund's second refund referenced no credit note; Ardennes Trail Co. rejected a Peppol invoice for a buyer reference the B2B portal never asked for. A merchant that accepts the claim makes the ERP the only invoice issuer, invoices per shipment and builds the shipped-not-invoiced list and the refunds-against-credit-notes job first, before an OMS or a PIM.
thesis.how_why: Rates depend on the destination country, the product category and the buyer's status, and change, so rates kept in several channels drift apart. A tax basis recomputed after the address or a rate changes no longer matches what the customer was shown, so the basis is frozen on the order and any difference listed. For goods the supply happens at dispatch, per shipment, so an invoice that waits for the whole order waits for the slowest line. The law requires a consecutive number unique to each invoice and an issued invoice kept unchanged for years, which only one issuing system per legal entity can guarantee. Where two systems can refund, both can refund the same return, so refunds come from one writer. A payout nets payments, refunds, fees and chargebacks from different days, so it never equals a day's sales and can be matched only line by line on identifiers carried from the order.

role.contribution: Follows the order into the documents that finance and the tax authorities rely on, extends the one-writer and key rules to invoices and credit notes, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with the hand-off to Part IV only).

transition_in.introduces: The tax it carries, the invoice each shipment produces and the entries those documents post in the books.

parts.title: Part IV — FULFILLMENT: From Warehouse to Doorstep and Back

know: The systems that witness Part IV's physical facts and what each writes: the warehouse system (on-hand stock, shipment confirmations, its cut-off, capacity and backlog), the carrier (scans of the parcel), the store's till (store stock and store sales) and the returns bench (the disposition of what came back).

How the order record instructs the place that does the work through a fulfillment order it accepts or rejects, and why the shipping status the customer sees is derived from carrier events mapped to one small vocabulary.
believe: A delivery date, a collection time or a refund is a promise computed from, or released by, an event of the system on the spot, not a sentence on a page or a status set by another system.
Notifications, the status page and the agent's screen must read one order record; a difference between them is a defect that reaches the customer as a contact.
can_do: For one order at their own company, name the system that witnesses each physical fact (stock on the shelf, the parcel's whereabouts, store stock, what came back), the event each customer-facing promise or message reads, the single writer of each refund and restock, and the measure that would show a broken promise.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given four broken promises after checkout, a reader who has read only Part IV names for each the fact that was taken from a copy or a sentence instead of from the system that witnessed it, or the action two systems could take, before naming a faster warehouse, a new till or more support staff.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shop's page says 'ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow' while on a busy evening orders reach the warehouse three hours late; a store-collection order is promised from last night's copy of store stock and the item is gone; a customer is refunded by support after the tracking shows the return 'delivered to warehouse' and again by the returns portal after inspection; a two-parcel order reads 'Delivered' after the first parcel. Using only Part IV: what was missing in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The promise was a sentence, not computed from the warehouse's cut-off and backlog (a queue whose age moves the cut-off); store stock was promised from a nightly copy with no per-store buffer and no staff confirmation before 'ready' (store stock should reach availability as events from the till); two systems could refund, the refund was released by a carrier scan rather than the warehouse's disposition, and the requests carried no return id as key; the order had one status word instead of goods state per shipment, so nothing emitted 'ships in two parcels' and the page and the agent did not read one record. Not 'a faster warehouse', 'a new POS' or 'more agents' alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the part's incidents against the opening's order confirmed in seconds and still to be picked, and states what they have in common; it does not only hand off to Part V.

thesis.question: Once the order is placed, how are the promises made about it (a delivery date, a collection, a return and its refund, the status the customer sees) kept?
thesis.claim: Promises about a placed order are kept only where each physical fact has one system that witnesses and writes it (the warehouse system, the store's till, the carrier, the returns bench) and that applies each instruction once, as a keyed request it accepts or rejects; where each promise is computed from that system's events or released by its confirmation; and where the customer and the service agent read one status built from those events.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that fulfillment is operations' work rather than architecture: once checkout has taken the order and the money, promises are kept by enough pickers, reliable carriers and helpful agents, and the storefront's delivery sentence, the shop platform's order status and its default refund flow are enough.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's four Part IV incidents were promises made without the witness's facts or acted on by more than one system: the Queue That Waited (roughly 8,000 Black Friday orders missed next-day delivery while the page promised it), the Store Stock Mirage (37 collection items already sold), the Double Refund (212 returns, €19,400) and the Three-Status Order (11 tickets). A merchant that accepts the claim names the witness and the writer of each physical fact, and the event each promise reads, before it buys a faster warehouse, a new till or more service capacity.
thesis.how_why: The storefront promises in seconds; the physical work happens hours or days later in buildings and vans the order record cannot see, and its facts (an empty pick location, a unit sold at the till, a parcel scan, a worn jacket on the bench) are known first by the system on the spot and reach the others by message, late or twice. A promise read from a copy or a static sentence is wrong whenever the copy lags or the queue grows; a status set by one integration overwrites what others know; and an action that two systems can take, such as a refund, is taken twice.

supporting_claims.claim: Each physical fact has one system that witnesses it and is its only writer: the warehouse system for on-hand stock at the warehouse, the till for store stock and store sales, the carrier's scans for the parcel's whereabouts and the returns bench's disposition for what came back; every other system holds a copy fed by that system's events.

The order record instructs the place that does the work through a fulfillment order that the place accepts or rejects and that carries a key, so a repeated instruction creates no second pick; after acceptance a cancellation or an edit is a request the place answers, and self-service and agents' actions check that state first.

A promise about time or place is computed from the warehouse's cut-off, capacity and backlog, the stock's location and the carrier's measured transit time per lane, with a buffer and a margin, and a promise against store stock becomes a commitment only when a person at the store confirms it.

On the way back, the warehouse's disposition is the event that releases the refund and the restock, and one system issues the refund with the return id as its key, whether the return started in the portal, at a store counter or on a marketplace.

The customer and the agent see one status, derived from these events and kept in one order record as separate goods (per shipment), money and return states; the notifications, the status page and the agent's view are read models over that record.

role.contribution: Shows the keeping side of the promise: warehouse, delivery, stores, returns and service.

additional_patterns.applies_to: warehouse-and-fulfillment, shipping-and-delivery and returns-and-exchanges: Eva's jacket out and back (picked at Duiven on 14 April 2027, delivered on 15 April, returned for size L from 19 to 22 April); stores-and-omnichannel sits between delivery and return as the alternative routes for the same order; customer-service-and-notifications spans 13 to 22 April

flow.rationale: Each chapter uses what the one before it fixed. The warehouse comes first because it defines the fulfillment order, the warehouse system as the writer of on-hand stock, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog; the shipping chapter computes the delivery promise from those three and adds the carrier's events and one vocabulary for them; the stores chapter reuses the fulfillment order, labels and carrier pickup for ship-from-store and the computed promise for collection, and adds the till as a second witness of stock and orders; the returns chapter needs the carrier's 'delivered' event, which starts the 14-day clock, the warehouse's receiving and stock events, and the store-return rule the stores chapter set, and adds the returns bench's disposition as the witness of what came back; the service chapter comes last because its messages, status page and agent view read the events every earlier chapter defined. Putting shipping before the warehouse would ask the reader to compute a promise from a cut-off and backlog not yet explained; putting stores before shipping would describe ship-from-store and the collection promise before labels, carrier pickup and the computed promise exist; putting returns before stores would leave its store-return section pointing forward; putting service earlier would describe messages for events whose emitters the reader has not met and would leave the part without the chapter that joins its events into one status.

hook.content: Checkout confirms an order in seconds, but someone still has to pick and pack the goods before the carrier's collection, and a late instruction or an empty shelf can push delivery back a day.

opening.bridge: From the confirmation the shopper sees in seconds to the physical work that follows over days, in a warehouse, a van, a store and on a returns bench; and to Eva's jacket: bought on 13 April 2027, picked and packed at Duiven on 14 April, delivered on 15 April, a day later than promised, size L requested on 19 April, the return inspected and the replacement shipped on 22 April, with store pickup and a counter exchange as the alternative routes.
opening.roadmap: Five chapters: the work instruction and response between order management and the warehouse (the Queue That Waited, a four-hour Black Friday backlog); carrier integration and credible delivery dates (Eva promised Wednesday and delivered Thursday); a step aside from Eva's parcel to the alternative routes through a store, with the till as another source of orders, stock and customer records (Utrecht's 37 items already sold); the return request, inspection, stock decision and money movement as separate states with owners (Eva's exchange, the 212 double refunds); messages, the status page and the support view built from shared facts (eleven tickets and the missing 'ships in two parcels').

closing.synthesis: The Queue That Waited, Eva's Wednesday promise, the Store Stock Mirage, the Double Refund and the eleven tickets look like five problems in five places: the warehouse feed, the storefront's text, store stock, refunds and support. Read together they are one: a promise or a status taken from a copy or a sentence instead of from the system that witnessed the physical fact, or an action two systems could take. Each chapter's remedy has the same parts: name the witness, compute the promise from its events and let a confirmation or a disposition commit it, give each money or stock action one writer and a key, and build one status from the same events.
closing.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's remedies are contracts and rules more than buildings or tills: a queue allowed to grow and a cut-off that moves with it, a transit table plus the warehouse's cut-off and backlog measured per lane, a two-unit store threshold and a staff confirmation, refund on disposition by one writer keyed on the return id, and the helpdesk pointed at the order hub; the till decision waits until 2028. A reader can list, for their own operation, which system witnesses each physical fact and which promise reads it.
closing.callback: The part opening's order confirmed in seconds whose goods still have to be picked and packed before the carrier's collection.

takeaway.content: For each promise your shop makes after checkout (delivery date, collection, refund, order status), name the system that witnesses the fact it depends on, the event that carries that fact, and the measure that shows when the promise broke; start with promised-versus-delivered per lane and contacts per split shipment.

transition_in.carries_over: The order record and the payment taken.
transition_in.introduces: The physical work that has to match the record: picking, shipping, delivery and the way back.

posts.question: What happens to an order inside the warehouse, and what must the warehouse system receive from, and report to, the rest of the platform?

know: The warehouse steps (receiving, put-away, slotting, wave or continuous release, picking, packing, shipping confirmation, cycle counting) and what each changes; where automation and robots sit beneath the warehouse system.

The fulfillment order and its lifecycle (requested, accepted or rejected, in progress, shipped, closed incomplete, with cancellation as a request), the warehouse's four interfaces, and the four ways to get warehouse execution (ERP module, dedicated WMS, 3PL, marketplace fulfillment program).
Why the SSCC label and the despatch advice (DESADV) are generated from pack confirmation.
believe: The warehouse system is the only writer of on-hand stock; every other system derives from its events.
Whether an order ships on time depends on when it reaches the warehouse and on the cut-off and backlog, not only on how fast people pick.
can_do: Specify the platform-to-WMS integration: what the fulfillment order carries, its key, the accept-or-reject answer, cancellation after acceptance, shipment confirmations, stock events and the reconciliation behind them.

A queue allowed to grow without failing checkout, order creation in batches within the rate limit, a monitor on the age of the oldest unprocessed order, and a cut-off that moves when that age grows. Not a faster warehouse or more pickers.

thesis.question: What happens to an order inside the warehouse, and what must the warehouse system receive from, and report to, the rest of the platform?
thesis.claim: Inside the warehouse an order becomes work that is released, picked, packed and confirmed as a shipment within the building's capacity and before the carrier's collection. The warehouse system must receive a fulfillment order it can accept or reject, carrying only what to ship and a key, so that a retried request creates no second pick list. As the only writer of on-hand stock, it must report shipment confirmations built from what was packed, every stock change as an event, and its cut-off, capacity and backlog.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that 'send the order to the WMS' is the whole specification: the warehouse receives the order as the shop holds it, any system may correct stock figures, and on-time dispatch is a matter of warehouse staffing and speed.
thesis.so_what: On Black Friday 2026 Duiven had the staff, but orders took four hours to reach its warehouse system and roughly 8,000 orders placed between 17:00 and midnight missed next-day delivery while the storefront promised it; the remedy was a queue, batches, a monitor on the oldest order and a moving cut-off, not a faster warehouse. Bergzicht deducted €14,200 because the despatch advice was built from the ERP's order rather than from what was packed. A merchant that accepts the claim writes the fulfillment-order contract, names the one writer of on-hand stock and feeds the cut-off to the promise before it buys a WMS, a 3PL or robots.
thesis.how_why: Physical work cannot be undone by changing a status: once the warehouse has accepted an instruction, picking may have started, so a cancellation needs the warehouse's answer. Prices, payments and customer history change for reasons the warehouse cannot act on and add data it must protect, so the instruction carries only what to ship. A request retried after a timeout arrives twice and, without a key, creates a second pick list. Only the warehouse counts shelves, so any second writer of on-hand stock produces phantom stock. An order that reaches the warehouse after the last wave ships the next day whatever the page said, so the promise must read the cut-off and the backlog. A pallet's SSCC and contents exist only at pack time, so the despatch advice must come from pack confirmation.

posts.title: Getting It There: Carriers, Labels, Tracking and the Delivery Promise
posts.question: How does a merchant connect to its carriers for labels and tracking, and how does it make a delivery promise it can keep?

know: The shipping vocabulary (carrier, service, label, manifest, tracking event, pickup point, cut-off, lane, estimated delivery date, rate shopping, multi-carrier platform) and the three moments shipping touches an order: the promise at checkout, the label at packing and the tracking after collection.
The four ways to talk to carriers and the four ways to make the promise (static rule, transit table, promise service, predictive model), with what each needs and is blind to.
What consumer law sets around delivery: 30 days unless agreed, risk with the merchant until possession, refund of only the cheapest standard delivery.
believe: From the second carrier onward a normalizing layer between the merchant's systems and the carriers is necessary; the choice is whether to buy or build it.
A promise that is not computed cannot be measured, and the only on-time rate to trust is the one computed from the merchant's own scan history.
can_do: Specify a first delivery-promise component: its inputs, its safe default when it is unavailable, and the promised-versus-delivered measure per lane.
Say what stops one parcel from getting two barcodes and what alerts on a missed manifest.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an order placed after the warehouse's last wave under a static next-day promise, the reader gives the date that should have been shown and the inputs that compute it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch storefront shows 'ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow'. A customer orders at 21:14 on a Tuesday; the warehouse released its last wave at 21:00, the carrier collects at 22:30, and transit on her lane is one day. Using only this chapter: what date should she have been shown, why, and what does showing it require?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Thursday, not Wednesday: the order ships on Wednesday because it missed the last wave, and transit adds one day. It requires a promise computed from the warehouse's cut-off and backlog, the stock's location, the lane's transit time and a margin, and measured as promised-versus-delivered per lane; not a reworded sentence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a retried label call and parcels that never left 'label created', the reader names each fault and its prevention.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A label call times out and is retried; later that day a batch of labeled parcels is collected but still shows only 'label created' in tracking. Using only this chapter: what went wrong in each case, and what prevents it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The retry booked a second shipment, giving one parcel two barcodes, because the call carried no merchant shipment reference; make the call idempotent by that reference and look up before creating. The second batch was never manifested: a label is not a booking until the day is closed with the carrier; make the close-out a scheduled job with an alert and watch for parcels stuck in pre-transit.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the order's shipping status should be derived from when several carriers use different codes.
